kurz: What the defensive part of a portfolio is for, why it offered no protection in 2022 and how to build it in practice.

bloecke.md:
The defensive part of a portfolio is not there to make money. Its job is to make the equity allocation bearable, and that can be quantified. A backtest of the classic 60/40 portfolio in US dollars (60% US stock market, 40% US bond market) arrives at 9.55% a year for the ten years to 31 August 2026. The standard deviation was 10.45%, and the maximum drawdown in those ten years was 20.69% (January to September 2022). In the financial crisis from November 2007 to February 2009, the same portfolio lost 30.55%. The MSCI World, by contrast, lost as much as 57.46% at its worst between October 2007 and March 2009, with a ten-year volatility of 14.86%.

The 40% bond allocation therefore costs return. In exchange, the low point stays limited enough for an investor to endure it without selling at the bottom. Whether this trade-off is worthwhile depends less on the statistics than on when the money is needed.

## Three jobs of the defensive part

The **stabiliser** reduces the volatility of the overall portfolio. For this it is enough that it fluctuates little itself. Whether it rises when equities fall is of secondary importance.

The **diversifier** is meant to gain when equities slump. Only a security whose price rises when interest rates fall can do this, that is, a government bond of good credit quality with meaningful [[Duration|duration]].

The **liquidity reserve** must be available in full on a specific date. For it, duration is the main risk. Anyone who has to make a down payment in eighteen months cannot wait for prices to recover.

The three jobs call for three different securities. A single product that is supposed to do all three does none of them reliably.

bloecke.titel: Correlation with US equities, monthly returns 01/2008 to 08/2026
bloecke.unter: Measured using ETF proxies (SHY, TLT, AGG, LQD, VNQ) against US large caps; the lower the value, the stronger the diversification.

bloecke.md:
The ranking shows that the safer and less volatile a security is, the better it diversifies. At 0.45, corporate bonds of good credit quality already move noticeably with the stock market, and at 0.75 real estate shares move almost in step with it. The extra yield on both depends on the same economic cycle as share prices. Investors who look for yield in the defensive part therefore usually bring equity risk into the portfolio, but without the upside potential of a share.

The same applies to foreign currencies. With a bond from the dollar area, currency fluctuation is often greater than interest rate and credit risk combined. For the stabilising part of a euro portfolio, currency-hedged securities or euro securities are therefore the norm.

The value of minus 0.07 between equities and long-dated government bonds is the average over 18 years. It contains two very different market phases. In 2008 and 2020 equities fell while bonds rose; in 2022 both fell together. Bonds protect against a recession but not against inflation, and you do not know in advance which of the two will occur.

## 2022 as a counterexample

The yield on ten-year German federal bonds rose in 2022 from minus 0.21% to plus 2.53%, an increase of 274 basis points in twelve months. As a result, a ten-year zero-coupon bond lost around 22% of its price over the year on paper. With an immediate jump in interest rates of this size, it would have been 23.7%. In the same year the MSCI World fell 17.73% (gross, in US dollars). Measured in euros, the loss was 12.34%, because the dollar gained against the euro. Both losses had the same trigger, the inflation shock. Such a shock raises the discount rate used to discount both future coupons and future corporate profits. If both asset classes depend on the same discount rate, they fall together when it rises.

Assume a euro portfolio of 60% global equities and 40% euro government bonds with a modified duration of 7 and a coupon close to zero, as was usual in the market at the end of 2021.

- Equity part (MSCI World in euros): 0.60 × (−12.3%) = −7.4 percentage points
- Bond part: −7 × 2.74 percentage points ≈ −19% in price, so 0.40 × (−19%) = −7.6 percentage points
- Total: around −15%

In practice convexity makes the loss somewhat smaller, but that does not change the order of magnitude. In that year, the defensive part therefore increased the loss instead of cushioning it.

A price loss on a bond is not final, because it is offset by higher returns in the future. Investors who stay invested for at least as long as the duration indicates recover the loss through higher reinvestment rates. This is why today's yield to maturity is the best estimate of the future return of a bond allocation. After a bad year, this yield is correspondingly high.

## Maturity of the defensive part

In the defensive part, it is above all the maturity that affects return and risk. On 18 September 2026, German federal bonds with a remaining maturity of two years yielded 3.24%, with ten years 3.52% and with thirty years 3.83%. For 28 additional years of commitment, the market therefore pays 0.59 percentage points more, while the price risk rises many times over.

bloecke.titel: Price impact of a one percentage point rise in interest rates
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation using the duration rule of thumb for a bond with a 2.5% coupon at a market yield of 3.52%; duration rises with maturity, but ever more slowly.

bloecke.titel: Return and interest rate risk of German federal bonds on 18 September 2026

bloecke.md:
The duration column is an illustrative calculation for a security with a 2.5% coupon at a uniform market yield of 3.52%; the yields are Bundesbank market data. The last two columns are deliberately shown as symmetrical. When interest rates fall, however, the gain is somewhat larger than the loss when rates rise. This difference is due to convexity.

A useful rule follows from this: the duration of the defensive part should roughly match the point in time when the money will be needed. Thirty-year bonds do not stabilise a portfolio. Investors who buy them for this purpose are making a big bet on interest rates. If interest rates rise by one percentage point, such a bond loses almost 20% of its market value according to the rule of thumb, and just over 17% when calculated exactly.

## ETF, individual bond or ladder

A bond ETF usually has no maturity. The fund sells securities that have become short-dated and buys new ones, so its duration stays roughly constant. You therefore never get the face value back with certainty on a fixed date. Many investors misjudge the asset class on this point. Target maturity ETFs such as the iBonds from iShares work differently; they hold only bonds maturing in a single year and are wound up afterwards. The two most important figures can be found in the factsheet: the effective duration and the yield to maturity. For AGG (iShares Core U.S. Aggregate Bond ETF), one of the largest US bond ETFs, they stood at 5.75 years and 5.23% in September 2026. At the same time, year-to-date performance was minus 0.99%, because interest rates continued to rise in 2026. A high expected return and negative current performance are therefore not mutually exclusive.

bloecke.titel: Four options for the defensive part

bloecke.md: The **bond ladder** solves the problem that both extremes have. Instead of a single maturity or none at all, it spreads the money across several maturity years. Each year one rung matures, the money is available as planned, and if it is not needed, you reinvest it at the long end of the ladder. This averages the interest rate level over the years, and you never have to decide whether today is a good time to buy. The drawback is the effort. Sensible diversification requires several securities, and with corporate bonds minimum denominations often make buying difficult.

schritte.titel: Set the amount and the number of rungs
schritte.text: For example, €50,000 across five rungs of €10,000 each, maturing from 2027 to 2031.

schritte.titel: Only buy credit quality that needs no checking
schritte.text: For the defensive part, that means German federal securities or equally safe euro government bonds. Credit risk belongs in the equity part.

schritte.titel: Roll over the maturing rung every year
schritte.text: The repaid amount is reinvested at the long end, so in 2027 in a bond maturing in 2032. The average duration of the ladder stays roughly the same.

schritte.titel: Before each reinvestment, check whether the money is needed
schritte.text: A ladder also serves as a withdrawal plan. If a car is to be bought in three years, the 2029 rung is not reinvested when it matures.

## Instant-access savings as an alternative

Since 16 September 2026, the ECB deposit facility rate has been 2.50%. Rates on instant-access savings accounts are guided by it but follow with a delay and incompletely. Top offers of around 4% in September 2026 were without exception promotions for new customers with a rate guarantee of three to six months, after which the rate usually drops significantly. Your own calculations should therefore be based on the deposit facility rate, not on promotional rates.

bloecke.titel: 2.50% instant-access savings after tax and inflation
bloecke.unter: Deduction of flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) and solidarity surcharge (26.375%, excluding church tax) and of German inflation for September 2026; if capital income stays below the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000, the tax step does not apply.

bloecke.md:
The real return after tax is therefore around minus 1.5%. This only partly applies to longer maturities. The 3.52% on the ten-year Bund comes to around 2.59% after tax. It must be compared with expected inflation over ten years, not with today's inflation rate of 3.3% (September 2026). The ECB projects 3.0% for the euro area in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028.

Instant-access savings and bonds differ above all in how long the interest rate is fixed, less in the level of the rate. Instant-access savings pay a variable rate. If the ECB cuts its rates, the previous rate no longer applies as early as the following month. A five-year bond locks in today's rate for five years, but its price fluctuates during that time. For an emergency fund the variability does not matter; for a pension gap in twelve years it is the central problem.

## Criticism of the age rule

“Bond allocation equals your age” or “100 minus your age in equities” is a rule of thumb with no theoretical basis. It is often cited as though it were a result of portfolio theory, but it is not one. An allocation can be soundly justified on the basis of human capital rather than age. Someone who will draw a secure salary for another thirty years already owns a large bond-like asset and can bear more equity risk in the portfolio. A self-employed person with fluctuating income, by contrast, has equity-like human capital and therefore a completely different need for stability at the same age.

For German investors there is a second point. The statutory pension is a lifelong, regularly adjusted stream of payments and thus acts like a very large bond position that does not show up in any portfolio statistics. A mechanical age-based allocation does not count it.

punkte: The investment horizon gets shorter with age
Losses shortly before withdrawal weigh more heavily than early losses
It forces you to set an allocation in the first place
Security of earned income and the statutory pension
Purpose of the money and timing of the payout
The investor's individual tolerance for losses
The interest rate level (in 2021 any bond allocation was expensive, in 2026 it is not)

bloecke.titel: Allocation by when the money is needed
bloecke.md: Money for the next three years belongs in an instant-access savings account or in bonds with maturities of less than two years. For money needed in three to ten years, a duration of roughly that period is appropriate, ideally as a ladder. Anything needed only after that belongs in the equity part. This way the allocation also shifts with age by itself, but for a comprehensible reason.

mitnehmen: The defensive part is meant to make the portfolio something you can stick with, and is therefore measured by the maximum drawdown of the overall portfolio, not by its own return.
Bonds protect against a recession but not against inflation; in 2022 equities and bonds fell together because both depend on the same discount rate.
The safer and less volatile a fixed-income security is, the better it diversifies; short-dated government bonds have a correlation with equities of minus 0.09, corporate bonds 0.45.
Duration should be based on when the money will be needed, not on expected return.
The age rule is a rule of thumb without a theoretical basis; an allocation can be justified via human capital and the time when the money will be used.

begriffe.text: Division of an amount across several maturity years. Each year one rung matures and, if not needed, is reinvested at the long end. This averages the interest rate level over time and spares you decisions about when to buy.

Interest rate sensitivity of a bond or bond fund in years, which also takes embedded options such as call rights into account (option-adjusted duration). For a fund with no maturity it stays roughly constant, because the fund continually replaces securities that have become short-dated with new ones. Such an ETF therefore has interest rate risk but no repayment date.

The risk of only being able to reinvest maturing amounts at lower interest rates. With instant-access savings it exists every day, with an individual bond it is concentrated at maturity, and with a ladder it is spread over the years.
Present value of future earned income. Secure earned income acts like a bond within total wealth and allows a higher equity allocation in the portfolio; insecure income acts like a share.
